procedural_history.impugned_order:
Judgments and Orders of the High Court of Judicature at Calcutta:
    * Dated 14th July, 1947, in Criminal Appeal No. 350 of 1946.
    * Dated 6th September, 1951, in Criminal Appeals Nos. 340, 341 and 351 of 1946 and Government Appeal No. 19 of 1946.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 350 of 1946, resulting in a Judgment and Order dated 14th July, 1947.  The High Court also heard Criminal Appeals Nos. 340, 341 and 351 of 1946 and Government Appeal No. 19 of 1946, resulting in a Judgment and Order dated 6th September, 1951. The High Court passed an order on August 2, 1948, adjourning an appeal until the disposal of the appeal of R.W. Mathams. The High Court passed an order on April 9, 1951, that remanded appeals would be heard on June 11, 1951.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court heard Criminal Appeals Nos. 9, 13, 14, and 15 of 1952. Criminal Appeal No. 9 came to the Supreme Court after a grant of Special Leave by the Privy Council on November 13, 1947, following the High Court's judgment and order dated July 14, 1947. Appeals under article 134 (l)(c) of the Constitution of India were also before the Supreme Court from the Judgment and Order dated the 6th September, 1951, of the High Court of Judicature at Calcutta in Criminal Appeals Nos. 340, 341 and 351 of 1946 and Government Appeal No. 19 of 1946.

issue.issue_text: Whether sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was necessary for instituting proceedings against the appellant on charges of conspiracy and bribery.

facts: The appellant was charged with conspiracy and bribery.
The appellant argued that the prosecution was invalid because it was initiated without obtaining the necessary sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
law: The court relied on the precedent set by two prior decisions of the Judicial Committee (Privy Council): H. H. B. Gill v. The King and Phanindra Chandra Neogy v. The King.
application: The court stated that the question of whether sanction under section 197 was necessary for charges of conspiracy and bribery was "now concluded" by the two cited decisions.
Instead of conducting a new analysis, the court simply followed the established precedent from those cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The court answered the question in the negative, holding that sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was not necessary for instituting proceedings against the appellant on charges of conspiracy and bribery.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code and a denial of a fair trial because the appellants did not have a reasonable opportunity to examine their witnesses.

facts: The appellants filed a list of 15 witnesses to be examined for the defence.
The court issued summons for these witnesses not in the manner prescribed by the Code, but by ordinary post.
When the case was taken up, it was found that this method had failed, as two summons had been returned and the status of the rest was unknown.
The Tribunal then passed an order refusing to issue any further process for the witnesses.
law: Section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code is an imperative provision that requires a court to issue process for defence witnesses unless it finds specific reasons for refusal, which were not present in this case.
If an accused, through no fault of their own, is not given a reasonable opportunity to adduce their evidence, there is no fair trial.
Rules of procedure designed to ensure justice must be scrupulously observed by the courts.
An accused cannot be convicted, even if the prosecution's case is strong, without being given an opportunity to present their evidence in rebuttal.
application: The Supreme Court affirmed the Federal Court's earlier finding that the Tribunal's refusal to issue process for the witnesses was a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
The evidence of the witnesses the appellants sought to call was considered material for refuting the charges of both conspiracy and bribery.
By declining to issue proper and further process for these witnesses, the Tribunal deprived the appellants of the opportunity to rebut the prosecution's case.
This denial of an opportunity to present their evidence meant the appellants did not receive a fair trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code and a denial of a fair trial. The court held that the appellants' convictions could not stand because they were condemned without being given a reasonable opportunity to present their evidence. The court emphasized that procedural rules ensuring justice must be strictly followed, and consequently, the convictions were set aside.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was a contravention of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code and a denial of a fair trial because the appellants did not have a reasonable opportunity to examine their witnesses.
appellant_arguments: The requirements of section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code were not met, resulting in an unfair trial.
The court failed to properly issue summons for their defence witnesses, sending them by ordinary post instead of the prescribed method, and then refused to issue further process when service failed.

The evidence from these witnesses was material, as it could have established the genuineness of key documents (Exhibit 27 series) and rebutted the prosecution's case on both conspiracy and bribery charges.
This failure deprived the appellants of the opportunity to present their evidence and rebut the prosecution's case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A conviction cannot stand if the accused was denied an opportunity to present their evidence, as this constitutes a failure of a fair trial. It is essential that rules of procedure designed to ensure justice are scrupulously followed, and a breach of such rules that deprives the accused of this opportunity will invalidate the conviction.
obiter: Whatever one may think of the merits of the appellants' contention, they cannot be convicted without an opportunity being given to them to present their evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Whatever one may think of the merits of the appellants' contention, they cannot be convicted without an opportunity being given to them to present their evidence, and that having been denied to them, there has been no fair trial, and the conviction of the appellants cannot stand. Even if the evidence on record tends to establish a strong case against the appellants, that is a case which they are entitled to rebut, and the court, by declining to issue process for the examination of material witnesses, deprived the appellants of that opportunity.
legal_tests_applied: Section 257 of the Criminal Procedure Code is imperative in its terms, and process for witnesses cannot be refused except for the specific reasons mentioned in the section.
why_appellant_lost: On the issue of sanction, the question of whether it was necessary under section 197 for charges of conspiracy and bribery is concluded by prior decisions of the Judicial Committee in H. H. B. Gill v. The King and Phanindra Chandra Neogy v. The King, and must be answered in the negative.
why_respondent_won: On the issue of sanction, the question of whether it was necessary under section 197 for charges of conspiracy and bribery is concluded by prior decisions of the Judicial Committee in H. H. B. Gill v. The King and Phanindra Chandra Neogy v. The King, and must be answered in the negative.
policy_considerations: It is essential that rules of procedure designed to ensure justice should be scrupulously followed, and Courts should be jealous in seeing that there is no breach of them, even if the result may be unfortunate.
